paragraphs: On the third day after East Pass closed its gates, the banner of Great Qin still flew above the walls.

At the morning change of guard, the soldiers formed two ranks behind the parapet, bowed southward toward the Heavenly King, and went to collect their millet cakes. By afternoon a basket of dates and two jars of clean water were lowered beside the gate. The commander called from the battlements, “Your Highness, Duke of Yangping, has come a long way. There are military matters to attend to within the city. Once the Duke of Beihai has given his approval, we shall certainly open the pass.”
Fu Rong had the water received. He left the dates untouched.

The two thousand central troops he had brought were encamped west of the imperial road, their tents pitched far apart. Cavalrymen tended their horses; infantrymen dug trenches. From a distance they might have been a garrison passing through. They had brought neither scaling ladders nor provisions for a long siege. If Fu Rong ordered an assault, the defenders facing him would be soldiers of Qin. If he turned and withdrew, the edict in his keeping—and Chang Xuan’s coffin—would be left without anyone to answer for them.

On the fifth day, the third messenger sent inside to inquire had still not returned. As the sun sank behind the battlements, Fu Rong went himself to a point beyond bowshot and called the commander’s name. The man had once fought beside him in Guanzhong. It took him a long time to show his face above the crenellations.
“I sent him to investigate Chang Xuan’s death,” Fu Rong called. “Where have you taken him?”
“By order of the Duke of Beihai, he has been sent on to Beidi for questioning.”
“What crime is he accused of?”
No answer came from the wall. After a while the commander said, “Your Highness would do well to withdraw your soldiers and wait for another express edict from the court.”

Fu Rong gave a short laugh, without the least amusement. “Here I stand. If you truly think this staff of the Heavenly King’s authority is a forgery, come down and examine it. If you know me, return my man. It isn’t the staff you cannot verify. It’s the bar across your gate.”
For a long time the wall was silent. In the gathering dusk, another beam was carried into the gatehouse and wedged across the doors.

That night a Beidi commandery clerk escaped by a mountain path. The soles of his shoes had worn through; both feet were blistered and bloody. He reported that the military registers Chang Xuan had left behind were under seal. Of the seventeen officers posted by the court, six had been dismissed, five confined in the relay station, and the rest forbidden to leave their camps. Veterans once discharged from the duke’s private service were returning, accepting their old armor but wearing the uniforms of the new army. The clerk’s voice trembled as he told the last part: the old private signals had been revived. Commandants no longer called the rolls by the Beidi camp register. They recognized men by the banners of their former households.

Fu Rong kept him beneath the lamp and gave him a bowl of hot gruel. Three times he asked where each camp gate stood, recording every answer word for word. Early the following morning he demanded the release of the detained messengers. From the watchtower the defenders lowered a strip of cloth bearing four characters: THE FRONTIER SITUATION REMAINS UNCLEAR.
At dawn on the sixth day, an urgent courier arrived from Chang’an.

He carried a palace gate token, and the mud of the relay road still stained his clothes. He presented an edict ordering Fu Rong to fall back fifty li and suspend his inspection of the troops in Beidi. The clay seal was intact; the paper was fine and white; the vermilion around the impression was of an even depth. Fu Rong read the edict twice, set it on the table, then brought out the document by which Chang Xuan had been appointed and handed it to his chief secretary.
“Read this passage.”
“Fu Luo, Duke of Beihai.”
“Now read the other.”
The secretary hesitated. “Fu Luo, Prince of Beihai.”

A silence settled over the tent. Fu Luo had never been raised to the rank of prince. Someone in the military secretariat suggested that His Majesty might have bestowed the title unexpectedly, with no time to announce it. Fu Rong did not argue. He asked the courier, “Which secretariat gentleman handed this to you?”

The courier gave a name, then recited his changes of horse along the relay stations without a single error. He even knew that Fu Rong had received a confidential summons before leaving the capital. The more smoothly he spoke, the more sweat gathered on the chief secretary’s brow. Fu Rong scarcely looked at the man. He folded the edict. “Please rest in the rear tent, sir. Take care not to lose your seal, your token, or your travel warrants.”
“Is Your Highness detaining me?”

“Chang Xuan trusted someone who offered to take him to inspect the beacon towers. What came back of him was a coffin.” Fu Rong raised his eyes. “Stay alive until I learn whether this edict is genuine.”

The following day another courier arrived, a gentleman of the Secretariat whom Fu Rong knew personally. The sight of the first messenger under guard drained the color from his face. He hastily unfurled an express edict from the Heavenly King: Fu Luo had privately recruited his former retainers, refused to admit officers appointed by the court, and concealed evidence concerning Chang Xuan’s murder. He was ordered to surrender his troops immediately. Every unit was to report to the Duke of Yangping within ten days; those who submitted voluntarily would be treated with leniency.

The two edicts lay side by side on a low table. In the candlelight their vermilion seals seemed identical. One commanded him to withdraw; the other, to advance. Beyond the tent, Qin’s war horns were still sounding, as though the world remained precisely what it had been yesterday.

Fu Rong questioned the messengers separately, with the tent wall between them. The first insisted he carried a secret command; the second maintained that the palace had never issued an order to withdraw. They disagreed so fiercely that they nearly began shouting abuse at each other. Fu Rong put them in separate custody, impounded their travel papers, and sent fast riders to Chang’an bearing letters under double seal. He did not send both original edicts away. Instead he took impressions of each seal and made careful records of the paper’s grain, dispatching the copies by different routes to the capital. Until their authenticity could be determined, the originals remained under two locks held by himself and his chief secretary.

Before noon, war drums suddenly sounded at East Pass. The commander lowered a transcript of another edict. It declared that the Heavenly King had been deceived by wicked ministers and had secretly ordered the Duke of Beihai to command the frontier garrisons, march on the capital, and purge the traitors beside the throne. The names listed included Quan Yi and Murong Chui—and, astonishingly, Fu Rong himself. Even the Crown Prince was dismissed as “too young to tell the loyal from the treacherous.” Fu Rong stared at his own name for a moment, then had the document passed to his youngest commandant.

The young officer had never seen the Heavenly King. What he knew of him came from the court’s seals and edicts. Now all those signs of authority were before him, and he no longer knew which way to point his sword.
“General,” he asked softly, “if this reaches the other camps…”
“It has,” Fu Rong said.

Within a day and a night, identical copies appeared in Beidi, Shangjun, and Anding. Some traveled through relay stations, some hidden in bales of leather goods; others were pasted to camp gates after dark. A small town south of Beidi received two incompatible commands. Its aging clerk dared not affix the commandery seal, and ordered the main gate bricked up that night. A neighboring garrison sent wagons of grain, only to find the gates closed. The carters complained that a dozen sacks of good grain were waiting in the road while the proper season for planting slipped away.

Some wanted to stand with Fu Luo, others to wait for Chang’an. Most dared to choose neither. The old frontier commanders feared something more than any edict: the possibility of having to acknowledge that what they had done before was wrong. So the officers at the passes barred their gates and refused to unlock them for messengers from either side.

At the Duke of Beihai’s residence, Fu Luo read the secret edict and rested a finger for a long time on the words PURGE THE TRAITORS BESIDE THE THRONE. He knew his elder brother would never order him to march against Fu Rong. No number of authentic seals in the world could have made him believe that.
His chief secretary urged him to order the army to obey. Fu Luo turned the bamboo slips facedown on the table. “Who brought this?”
“We don’t know. A fast rider delivered it to the relay station and left.”
“Did he come from Chang’an?”
“The horse and the travel papers are of the Chang’an pattern.”
“I asked about the man.”

The secretary had no answer. Instead he said that Fu Rong had already sent the order to surrender the troops to every garrison along the route. If the old camps relinquished their commands now, someone would have to answer for the concealed registers and for Chang Xuan’s death.

Fu Luo paced the chamber twice. Countless thin bamboo counters stood in the military map—mountain passes, relay roads, old encampments, places he had crossed in his youth. Once he had thought the bitterest wrong of his life was the court’s taking from him men who had bled beside him. Now Chang Xuan was dead, the messengers were detained, and East Pass was shut. He could no longer say at which step the soldiers he commanded had become something he was afraid to release.
“Send the copies to every camp,” he said at last.

A look of pleasure had barely reached the secretary’s face when Fu Luo added, “Do not say they are orders to march. Say only that I ask the generals to examine them. If anyone adds a single word in my name, execute him.”

The secretary assented. There was no smile on his face as he left. Fu Luo looked toward a half-dead scholar tree beyond the window and felt that he had failed to finish what he meant to say. What, exactly, were the generals supposed to examine? Who would admit that an edict capable of washing away his crimes was false?

That night Qin banners rose above the camps of Beidi, with an extra strip of white cloth tied to the corner of each. The cloth had originally been prepared for the cart that bore Chang Xuan to burial. Now men were calling it the emblem of a purge of the court. Fu Luo heard what they were saying and gave no order to take it down.

The impressions of the two conflicting edicts reached the palace in Chang’an close to midnight. The Secretariat’s old archives were carried into Chengming Hall and stacked higher than a man. Fu Jian opened the register of seal impressions and asked the keeper whether an old seal remained in storage. At first the man said no. Then he remembered a bronze seal, damaged at one corner in the reign of the previous king, that had been locked away in the inner treasury. He fell to the floor in terror. Fu Jian did not have him beaten. He ordered the treasury sealed that night, with no one permitted to approach it alone.

Yao Chang, commander of the Right Guard, entered the hall in armor and requested permission to seal the palace gates and check everyone passing through. His proposals were comprehensive. He even suggested that the Crown Prince lead the Judicial Commandant’s investigation of the treasury, while Yao himself merely posted guards along the outer corridors. Quan Yi studied him for several moments. Fu Jian asked if anyone objected. Quan Yi replied, “The gates must be guarded. But the investigators must not all be made to pass through the same gate.”

Accordingly the Right Guard held the palace’s outer passages for the time being, while the Secretariat, the seal chamber, and the inner treasury each received gate tablets from the Crown Prince’s Guard and the Judicial Commandant. Every entry and exit had to be entered in the records of both offices. Yao Chang accepted the order at once. On his way out he paused at the threshold and bowed to Fu Hong. “Your Highness, the palace holds all manner of people. I hope you will take great care.”
Fu Hong began with the paper.

The genuine order to surrender the troops was slightly yellow, with fine impressions left by a bamboo screen. The forged order to withdraw was unnaturally white; at the lower right corner of the secret edict about purging the court, a pale water stain showed through. The storekeeper recalled that the Right Guard’s inner storehouse had once leaked in the rain, and that many of its older sheets bore similar marks. Twenty-seven sheets were missing from the accounts. A storehouse guard named Duan Cai had been executed for theft seven days earlier. The Right Guard had produced the record of his death under the rod, complete with seals and signatures.

The Judicial Commandant quietly ordered the grave opened. The dead man’s skull had been fractured at the back in a manner inconsistent with the severity of his recorded beating. Fu Hong examined the report and remembered Pu Sheng’s death in prison. Yet similarity was no proof that the same killer was responsible. He sealed Duan Cai’s deposition and first asked who had prepared the body and who had seen it. Only then did he order inquiries among the palace attendants who had shared his watch.

A lamp attendant named Gao Fu tried to leave the city that very night on hearing of the investigation. Fu Hong deliberately had the soldiers on duty spread word that suspicious evidence had been found in the Secretariat’s paper store. He then set watchers on those coming and going from the Right Guard’s quarters. After dark a personal guard left the palace and turned into a deserted office. An attendant emerged from its back gate, went to a leather merchant in the western market to collect a trader’s clothing and gold coins, then headed for a mule-and-horse yard outside the city. Officers of the Judicial Commandant stopped the wagon before it could pull away. Among the things they seized was a cloth strip marked with the names of relay stations.

In a private chamber, Gao Fu insisted he had merely been trying to save his life. Fu Hong did not hurry him. He showed him Duan Cai’s examination report and asked, “Was this man beaten to death, or was he struck on the head beforehand?”

Gao Fu pressed his lips together. The Crown Prince spread the account of the missing paper before him. “If all you took was paper, then tell me you took paper. You need not claim another man’s blood as your own.”
Gao Fu looked up sharply. “I never carved a seal!”
The moment he spoke, he clapped a hand over his mouth in horror. The Crown Prince laid down his brush without pressing him further. “You saw the seal?”

After a long silence Gao Fu nodded. He did not know the name of the person who had collected the paper. He said only that a man who walked slightly slower on his right foot had asked him, from behind a curtain, when the keys to the inner treasury would next be brought together. Fu Hong recorded the words “behind a curtain,” then ordered that Gao Fu be shown no suspects and that no soldier of the Right Guard be allowed near him. So vague an impression could not yet serve as an identification.

The attendant responsible for the night water clock came to report the fifth watch. Only then did Fu Hong notice that his lamp was nearly spent. He had not slept in a day and a night. He remembered how, when his father had first taken him into the Secretariat the year before, he could scarcely distinguish an error in a grain voucher. Now twenty-seven sheets of paper were enough to make frontier cities kill one another. Afraid that he was beginning to mistake a clue for an answer, he summoned two other officers of the Judicial Commandant to examine the paper independently and forbade them to read Gao Fu’s testimony beforehand.

At dawn Yao Chang came to pay his respects and ask whether the investigation had made progress. Fu Hong said there were several Secretariat scribes he needed to locate. Yao offered to send the Right Guard to look for them. The Crown Prince answered, “General, you still have the palace gates to tend. The Judicial Commandant will find the missing scribes.” They parted with all the proper courtesies. Yao Chang’s steps became a little more deliberate as he passed down the corridor.

As he left the palace, Yao heard that Gao Fu had been captured. He said nothing at first. A military officer at his side asked whether they should still retrieve the old paper from the storehouse. Yao turned, as though hearing of the matter for the first time. “Which storehouse?”

The officer lowered his eyes and did not ask again. Yao took hold of his reins and looked at the clerks newly posted beside the gate to inspect entry tablets. Then he smiled faintly. Fu Hong had not removed him from command, but there was another pair of eyes at every door.

In Beidi, strips of white cloth still fluttered beneath the Qin banners. Fu Rong stood outside East Pass and listened to the night wind worrying the flag ropes. He could not know behind which edict the commander within—the man who had once defended the border at his side—had chosen to stand that night.
